summary: Defines the Certification Authority Authorization DNS record, which lets a domain holder list the certification authorities allowed to issue certificates for that name. Public CAs can check it to reduce the risk of mis-issued certificates. The document specifies the record syntax and the rules for processing it. It obsoletes RFC 6844.

eli5.summary: A house owner can put up a notice saying only these locksmiths may make keys for this door. A certificate company checks the notice first.

questions: how to restrict certificate issuance for a domain
subtitle: A DNS record that lets a domain holder say which certificate authorities may issue certificates for that name.

tldr.problem: Anyone running a domain wants to limit which certification authorities (CAs) can issue certificates for it, to reduce the risk of unintended mis-issue.
tldr.mechanism: The domain publishes CAA resource records. Before issuing, a CA looks up the Relevant RRset by climbing the DNS name tree and must not issue unless the request is consistent with it.
tldr.outcome: CAA reduces the risk of mis-issue but cannot stop an authorized CA from mis-issuing. RFC 8659 obsoletes RFC 6844 with a simpler lookup algorithm.

today: RFC 8659 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 6844, so it is the current definition of the CAA record.

sections.title: What CAA Is For
sections.content:
The Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS resource record lets a domain name holder name the CAs allowed to issue certificates for that domain. A public CA can use it as an extra control against unintended mis-issue.

The RFC contrasts CAA with the TLSA record from DANE (RFC 6698). CAA is an authorization control that the CA performs before issuing. TLSA is a verification control that a relying party performs after issuance. Conforming to a published CAA record is necessary but not sufficient for issuing a certificate.

CAA records describe only current grants of authority. A certificate may have been valid under the records of its day and not match today's. So relying parties MUST NOT use CAA records in certificate validation. Certificate evaluators MAY treat a mismatch as a possible sign of a policy violation, allowing for records that changed since issuance.
sections.eli5: The notice on the door says who may make new keys. It does not tell you whether an old key was fine, because the notice may have changed since then.

sections.title: Finding the Relevant Records
sections.content:
Before issuing, a compliant CA MUST check for a Relevant RRset. If one exists, the CA MUST NOT issue unless the request is consistent with it, or an exception in the CA's Certificate Policy or Certification Practices Statement applies. If the RRset has no tags that restrict issuance (for instance only iodef tags, or tags the CA does not recognize), CAA does not restrict issuance. A request can name several names and wildcard names, and the CA must verify all of them.

The search starts at the requested name and climbs the DNS name tree, up to but not including the root, until a CAA RRset is found. For A.B.C with a record issue example.com at B.C, the search stops at B.C. For a wildcard *.X, the lookup starts from X.

Only the name being processed is climbed. Aliases are followed by the lookup itself, following the algorithm in RFC 1034.
sections.eli5: The CA looks for a notice at your door. If there is none, it checks the building, then the street, going up until it finds one or runs out of places.

sections.title: The Record Format
sections.content:
Each CAA record holds one Property, a tag and value pair. A name can have several records, and a tag can appear more than once. The data has a one-octet Flags field, a one-octet Tag Length (at least 1), the Tag in ASCII, and the Value, which fills the rest of the data.

Tags may use letters a to z, A to Z and digits, and are matched case-insensitively. In presentation format a record looks like CAA <flags> <tag> <value>, with flags an unsigned integer from 0 to 255.

Bit 0 of Flags is the Issuer Critical Flag. If it is set, a CA MUST NOT issue for any name whose Relevant RRset has a critical property with an unknown or unsupported tag. Following DNS convention, bit 0 is the most significant bit, so the value 128 sets it. Reserved bits must be cleared by publishers and ignored by readers.
sections.eli5: Each notice is a short label with a tag, such as "issue", and a value, such as the name of the allowed locksmith.

sections.title: The issue, issuewild and iodef Properties
sections.content:
The issue property authorizes the holder of the named issuer domain, or someone acting under its explicit authority, to issue certificates for the name. A value of ; with no issuer asks that nobody issue. A value that does not match the grammar is treated like an empty issuer, so it forbids issuance. Authorizations are additive. An issuer may define parameters such as account=230123, whose meaning only that issuer decides.

The issuewild property has the same syntax but covers only wildcard names, and takes precedence over issue for them. It is ignored for non-wildcard requests. If any issuewild exists for a wildcard request, every issue property is ignored for it.

The iodef property gives a URL for reporting requests or issuances that break policy, using the IODEF format from RFC 7970. Only mailto:, http and https are supported.

The critical flag lets future CAA versions add semantics that CAs must understand. In the RFC's example, a record CAA 128 tbs "Unknown" blocks any CA that does not implement the tbs tag.
sections.eli5: One note says which locksmiths may make keys. Another says who may make keys for the double doors, which beats the first. A third says whom to tell if something looks wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CAA only helps if CAs obey it. It aims to reduce the risk of mis-issue, not to avoid relying on a certificate already mis-issued; DANE covers that. It does not stop an authorized CA from mis-issuing, so holders SHOULD check that the CAs they authorize have suitable controls.

Using DNSSEC for CAA records is strongly RECOMMENDED but not required. An issuer must not issue against the Relevant RRset whether or not it is signed. DNSSEC lets a CA tell an empty answer from a suppressed one, and allows it to keep proof of authorization. Without DNSSEC, suppressed or bogus records could let an attacker get a certificate from an unauthorized CA, so the CA should query authoritative nameservers and must not rely only on third-party caches.

The RFC judges the denial-of-service risk from malformed records to be small. It also notes that a CA might trick customers into publishing critical-flag records that block competitors, but calls the effect minimal because a competitor would investigate.
sections.eli5: The notice only works if the locksmiths read it honestly. A forged or torn-down notice could fool them, so a tamper-proof seal on it helps.

sections.title: Deployment Problems
sections.content:
The RFC lists common causes of lookup errors so that CAs can help their customers. Some middleboxes, especially anti-DDoS appliances, drop DNS packets of unknown types, which shows up as a timeout or a SERVFAIL at a local resolver. Some authoritative servers answer REJECTED or NOTIMP for unknown record types, and at least one sends a malformed response. The correct response code for an unknown type is 0, no error.

If a subdomain is delegated to a nameserver with a private address, the CA gets SERVFAIL and may treat that as preventing issuance. Administrators who want certificates for private names SHOULD use split-horizon DNS so the CA sees a valid, empty CAA answer.

With DNSSEC, a signed empty response means no CAA policy exists, while a bogus one may mean misconfiguration or tampering. At least two authoritative servers with live signing had bugs with empty answers combined with mixed-case queries (DNS 0x20), including PowerDNS before version 4.0.4.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the mail carrier cannot reach the door or gets confused by a strange envelope. Then the locksmith cannot read the notice and may refuse to cut a key.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 6844
sections.content:
The main change is the lookup. RFC 6844 climbed the tree for the name and also for every CNAME and DNAME met along the way, which was inefficient and made it hard for hosting providers to set policy on their own names without affecting customers. RFC 8659 climbs only the name being processed and leaves CNAME and DNAME handling to the CA's recursive resolver.

It also adds the Deployment Considerations section, clarifies the grammar for issue and issuewild (parameters are separated by semicolons, and hyphens are allowed in tags), and clarifies how to treat a non-empty RRset with no issue or issuewild tags. The IANA entries now point to RFC 8659 instead of RFC 6844.
sections.eli5: The old rules made the CA chase every forwarding sign it met. The new rules just walk up the one address.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bit 0 is the Issuer Critical Flag; other bits are reserved.

fields.name: Tag Length
fields.desc: Length n of the tag in octets; at least 1.
